latin.1628: LXXI. Sed ut ad Sacram Scripturam redeamus, non solum in ea nullum praeceptum aut exemplum de Angelorum, sive de Sanctorum mortuorum cultu reperitur, sed saepius ipsa docet unum Deum adorandum, & illi soli serviendum esse: adeoque nec Angelis, nec Sanctis in Christo defunctis religiosum ullum cultum esse deferendum. Respondent Scholae Romanae Doctores scripturam solum prohibere ne creaturis deferamus cultum illum summum atque absolutum, quo aliquis colitur, tanquam primum principium, atque ultimus finis, cui cultui Latriae nomen appropriaverunt, non vero prohibitum esse Dei Ministris & amicis, quales sunt Angeli, & justorum Spiritus in gloriam caelestem recepti, inferiorem illum religionis cultum quem ipsi Duliam appellant, exhibere.
latin.1629: LXXII. Verum Scriptura sacra, dum creaturas adorare & illis servire prohibet, non vetat simpliciter ne creaturas agnoscamus ut primum principium atque ultimum finem, easque sub hac ratione colamus; sed ne quovis praetextu exerceamus erga illas adorationis religiosae actus, quales sunt aliquem publice invocare, hymnos illi canere, incensum adolere, aedes sacras & festos dies dicare, per nomen ejus jurare, vota illi nuncupare, & quae sunt similia.
latin.1630: LXXIII. Rem autem ita se habere inde manifeste probatur, quod Ethnicorum sapientes arguuntur ab Apostolo, ut ii qui ἐσεβάσθησαν καὶ ἐλάτρευσαν τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα, id est, qui creaturam cultu divino coluerunt, praeter creatorem, sive potius quam creatorem: quia scilicet, Solem, Lunam, & Astra, Heroas, & Genios religiose colebant. Et tamen certum est, illos Ethnicorum sapientes Solem, Heroas, & Genios non pro summis Diis habuisse, sed pro Ministris summi illius Dei, quem vocabant Patrem hominumque Deumque, quemque etiam in divis illis inferioribus honorari existimabant. Rom. 1. 26.
latin.1631: LXXIV. Sic refert Orosius Paganos fateri solitos non se plures Deos sequi, sed sub uno Deo Magno plures Ministros venerari. Sic etiam vetus Recognitionum scriptor eosdem Paganos dicentes introducit, Unum esse & nos dicimus Deum qui est omnium Dominus. Sed & isti Dii sunt. Sicut enim unus est Caesar, & habet sub se multos judices, verbi gratia Praefectos, Consules, Tribunos, & caeteras Potestates; simili arbitramur modo, cum unus sit omnium Deus, etiam istos ad similitudinem earum, quas diximus Potestatum, ordinatos esse in hoc mundo Deos, illi quidem majori subjectos, nos tamen & quae in hoc mundo sunt dispensantes. Oros. histor. lib. 6. init. Clem. Recogn. lib. 5.
latin.1632: LXXV. Unde est quod Celsus apud Origenem affirmat Eum qui plures Deos veneratur, hoc ipso in quantum unum aliquem Deo maximo subditum colit, rem gratam summo Deo facere: & addit, Quod neminem honore prosequi licet, nisi quem ille honorari vult: quapropter qui veneretur ejus subditos non offendere illum cujus omnes sunt. Ideoque sic coli vult inferiores illas sub summo Deo potestates, Ut Deus nullo pacto unquam relinquatur, non noctu, non interdiu, non in privato, non in publico, non in cogitationibus ullis, non in operibus, sed sive cum his, sive sine his semper intenta sit ad Deum anima. Et postea, Sic, inquit, magnum Deum magis venerari videberis, si hos quoque hymnis honores & laudibus. Quibus consonum est quod docet Hierocles, Deos ita agnoscendos & colendos, ut sunt ab authore suo & parente distincti, non autem eorum dignitatem supra modum esse attollendam; denique cultum esse referendum ad eorum opificem unicum, quem Deum Deorum tanquam summum & optimum proprie nominare queas. Apud Orig. contra Cels. lib. 8. Hierocl. in carm. Pythag. pag. 10.
latin.1633: LXXVI. Proinde cum jam dicti Ethnicorum sapientes Solem, Lunam, & Genios inferiori duntaxat aliquo cultu coluerint, non tanquam Deos summos, sed solum tanquam summi Dei ministros, totumque istum cultum ad honorem ipsius summi Dei retulerint, ut ex allegatis testimoniis patet; & nihilominus ab apostolo dicantur creaturae λατρεῦσαι Latriam & cultum divinum exhibuisse creaturae, manifestum est eos non purgari a crimine Latriae Angelis & Sanctis defunctis exhibitae, qui colunt illos precibus & hymnis votis & juramentis per eorum nomen conceptis, oblationibus variis, aedibus sacris, & diebus festis eorum honori dicatis, etiamsi protestentur se omnia ista Sanctis & Angelis exhibere, non tanquam diis summis, sed tanquam Dei Ministris & amicis, adeoque Diis solum per participationem, idque relative ad Deum ipsum summum, in cujus honorem tandem ista cedant & referantur.
latin.1634: LXXVII. Neque est quod dicat aliquis Ethnicos ab Apostolo accusari Latriae creaturis exhibitae, quoniam obtulerunt eis sacrificia, quae omnium confessione ad Latriae cultum spectant. Nam Scriptura sacra non solum Gentes damnat quod creaturis immolarint, sed vel eo nomine quod illas osculo sacro coluerint. A quo crimine vir Sanctus Job protestatur se fuisse immunem, Si vidi, inquit, solem quum fulgeret, & lunam incedentem clare: Et laetatum est, sive potius seductum est in abscondito cor meum, & osculatus sum manum meam ore meo. Job. 31. 26.
latin.1635: LXXVIII. Adde quod, si juxta Doctorum Scholae Romanae hypotheses, licet creaturas etiam Latria, modo non absoluta, sed relativa colere, nulla solida ratio reddi potest, cur ipsis relative sacrificare non liceat. Et si bonum & pium est, Angelis & Sanctis cum Christo regnantibus vota nuncupare, & per eos jurare, quatenus illis Deus per gloriam inhabitat, & divina veritas in iis elucet, ac sunt Dii quidam per participationem, cur impium & prohibitum sit, eo nomine & respectu, sacrificia iisdem offerre. Neque etiam prisci Ecclesiae doctores sola sacrificia divino illi cultui, quem creaturis deferre nefas est, reservarunt, sed ut supra vidimus, preces quoque & hymnos, quos in solum Deum universorum Dominum dici volunt.
latin.1636: LXXIX. Verum Scriptura sacra non solum in genere dicit unum Deum esse colendum, & Latriam non esse creaturis exhibendam, sed etiam in specie vetat ne θρησκείαν ullam, id est, cultum ullum religiosum Angelis deferamus. Si autem non licet Angelos religiose colere, multo minus licebit cultum illum erga Sanctos defunctos adhibere; cum Angeli naturae praestantia homines superent, nec sint Sanctis gratia & gloria inferiores. Angelorum autem θρησκείαν, sive cultum religiosum expresse damnat Paulus Apostolus. Nemo, inquit, vos seducat volens in humilitate, & religione θρησκείᾳ Angelorum, quae non vidit ambulans, seu pedem inferens in ea quae non vidit, frustra inflatus sensu carnis suae. Ubi Apostolus simpliciter prohibet θρησκείαν, id est cultum religiosum Angelorum. Non potest autem ulla cum ratione negari illos θρησκεύειν, id est, religiose colere Angelos, qui aedes sacras in honorem Angelorum construunt, dies festos illis dicant, in locis religiosis solenniter eos invocant, & eorum patrocinium ac protectionem precibus ambiunt, ac quasi coram praesentibus atque intuentibus genua flectunt, & in terram procumbunt. Adeoque tales, secundum Pauli mentem, aut ab illis seducti sunt, aut temere sensu carnis suae inflati.
latin.1637: LXXX. Quod si quis ejusmodi cultus, ex Apostoli sententia Angelis debitus fuisset, si licitum existimavisset festa & Oratoria Angelis consecrare, & in publicis fidelium coetibus hymnos illis canere, eosque invocare, ac coram illis procumbere, non simpliciter damnasset Angelorum culturam, sed siquid immodicum in Angelorum religioso cultu apud Colossenses ab Impostoribus fuisset introductum, illud distincte notavisset, & legitimum Angelorum cultum ab illegitimo quadam ratione secrevisset: ut facerent proculdubio Doctores Scholae Romanae, siqua secta jam exoriretur, quae ipsorum judicio, nimium quid Angelis in hoc genere tribueret.

sections.title: Scripture: one God adored and served; the Roman reply of latria and dulia
sections.pass_a: But to return to Sacred Scripture, not only is no precept or example found in it concerning the worship of Angels or of dead Saints, but more often it itself teaches that one God is to be adored and that he alone is to be served: and so that no religious worship is to be offered either to Angels or to Saints who have died in Christ. The Doctors of the Roman School respond that scripture only forbids that we offer to creatures that highest and absolute worship by which someone is worshipped as first principle and last end, to which worship they have appropriated the name of Latria; but that it is not forbidden to show to God's Ministers and friends, such as are the Angels and the Spirits of the just received into heavenly glory, that lower worship of religion which they themselves call Dulia.
pass_b: But to return to Holy Scripture: not only does it contain no command or example concerning the worship of angels or of the dead saints, but it often teaches that one God is to be adored and that he alone is to be served. So no religious worship at all is to be given either to angels or to the saints who have died in Christ.

The teachers of the Roman school reply that Scripture forbids us only to give creatures that supreme and absolute worship by which someone is worshiped as first principle and last end, the worship for which they have reserved the name latria. It does not, they say, forbid us to show God's servants and friends, such as the angels and the spirits of the just received into heavenly glory, that lower religious worship which they call dulia.

lemmas.gloss: to which worship they have appropriated the name Latria
that lower worship of religion

choices.why: The Roman doctors restrict the word latria to supreme worship; 'reserved' gives the sense of claiming the term for one use only.

sections.title: What Scripture forbids: acts of religious adoration toward creatures under any pretext
sections.pass_a: But sacred Scripture, while it forbids to adore creatures and to serve them, does not simply forbid that we acknowledge creatures as first principle and last end and worship them under this aspect; but that under any pretext whatever we exercise toward them acts of religious adoration, such as are: to invoke someone publicly, to sing hymns to him, to burn incense, to dedicate sacred buildings and feast days, to swear by his name, to vow vows to him, and the things which are similar.
pass_b: When Holy Scripture forbids us to adore creatures and serve them, it is not merely ruling out that we should take creatures for the first principle and last end and worship them in that capacity. It rules out our performing, on any pretext at all, acts of religious adoration toward them: calling on someone in public worship, singing him hymns, burning incense, dedicating churches and feast days, swearing by his name, making vows to him, and the like.

lemmas.gloss: under this aspect (in that capacity)
to pronounce vows to him

choices.why: Sacred buildings dedicated in someone's honor; in seventeenth-century controversy these are churches and chapels.

sections.title: Romans 1: the pagan sages served the creature though they held it a minister of the supreme God
sections.pass_a: But that the matter is so is manifestly proved from this, that the wise men of the Heathen are accused by the Apostle as those who worshipped and served the creature beside the creator, that is, who worshipped the creature with divine worship, beside the creator, or rather than the creator: because namely they religiously worshipped the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars, Heroes and Genii. And yet it is certain that those wise men of the Heathen did not hold the Sun, the Heroes and the Genii for highest Gods, but for Ministers of that highest God whom they called Father of men and of Gods, and whom they also thought to be honored in those lower divinities. Romans 1:26 as printed (the words are 1:25).
pass_b: That this is how things stand is plainly proved by the Apostle's charge against the pagan philosophers: they "worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator," that is, they gave divine worship to the creature beside the Creator, or rather than the Creator, because they worshiped the sun, the moon and the stars, the heroes and the genii with religious worship (Romans 1:25).

Yet it is certain that those pagan philosophers did not take the sun, the heroes and the genii for supreme gods. They took them for servants of that supreme God whom they called the Father of men and gods, and whom they believed was honored also in those lesser divinities.

lemmas.gloss: beside / rather than the one who created
Father of men and of gods (Deum = deorum)

choices.term: praeter creatorem, sive potius quam creatorem
choices.english: beside the Creator, or rather than the Creator
choices.why: Le Blanc glosses Greek para both ways; the English keeps both senses.

notes: The 1675 print reads Rom. 1. 26; the words cited are Romans 1:25, so the English gives 1:25.

sections.title: Orosius and the Recognitions: pagans own one God with many ministers
sections.pass_a: Thus Orosius reports that the Pagans were accustomed to confess that they did not follow many Gods, but under one great God venerated many Ministers. Thus also the old writer of the Recognitions introduces the same Pagans saying: We too say that there is one God who is Lord of all. But these also are Gods. For as there is one Caesar, and he has under him many judges, for example Prefects, Consuls, Tribunes and the other Powers; in a similar way we think, since there is one God of all, that these also, after the likeness of those Powers which we named, have been ordained Gods in this world, subject indeed to that greater one, yet dispensing us and the things which are in this world. Orosius, Histories book 6 beginning; Clement, Recognitions book 5.
pass_b: So Orosius reports that the pagans used to say they did not follow many gods, but venerated many servants under one great God.

So too the old author of the Recognitions brings in the same pagans saying: "We also say that there is one God, who is Lord of all. But these too are gods. For just as there is one Caesar, who has many judges under him, such as prefects, consuls, tribunes and the other authorities, in the same way we think that, since there is one God of all, these too have been appointed gods in this world on the pattern of the authorities we have named. They are subject to the greater one, but they govern us and all that is in this world." (Orosius, Histories, book 6, beginning; Clement, Recognitions, book 5.)

lemmas.latin: nos tamen & quae in hoc mundo sunt dispensantes
lemmas.gloss: yet administering us and the things in this world

lemmas.latin: ordinatos esse in hoc mundo Deos
lemmas.gloss: to have been appointed gods in this world

choices.why: Dispensare is to manage or administer; the pagans make the lesser gods stewards of the world under the supreme God.

sections.title: Celsus and Hierocles: lesser powers honored so that the supreme God is never left
sections.pass_a: Hence it is that Celsus in Origen affirms that he who venerates many Gods, by this very thing, inasmuch as he worships some one subject to the greatest God, does a thing pleasing to the highest God: and he adds, That it is lawful to follow no one with honor except whom he wills to be honored: wherefore he who venerates his subjects does not offend him whose all are. And therefore he wills those lower powers under the highest God to be worshipped so, That God be in no manner ever abandoned, not by night, not by day, not in private, not in public, not in any thoughts, not in works, but whether with these or without these the soul be always intent toward God. And afterwards, Thus, he says, you will seem to venerate the great God more, if you honor these also with hymns and praises. With which agrees what Hierocles teaches, that the Gods are to be acknowledged and worshipped as they are distinct from their author and parent, but their dignity is not to be raised beyond measure; finally that worship is to be referred to their one maker, whom you may properly name God of Gods as highest and best. In Origen, Against Celsus book 8. Hierocles on the Pythagorean verses page 10.
pass_b: This is why Celsus, as Origen reports him, says that whoever venerates many gods does something pleasing to the supreme God by that very act, insofar as he worships one who is subject to the greatest God. He adds: "No one may be honored except those whom God wills to be honored; so whoever venerates his subjects does not offend him to whom all belong."

So he wants the lesser powers under the supreme God to be worshiped in such a way "that God is never in any way abandoned, not by night, not by day, not in private, not in public, not in any thought, not in any work, but that with these or without them the soul is always intent on God." Later he says: "In this way you will seem to venerate the great God the more, if you honor these too with hymns and praises." (Origen, Against Celsus, book 8.)

With this agrees what Hierocles teaches: "The gods are to be acknowledged and worshiped as distinct from their author and parent, but their dignity is not to be raised beyond measure; in the end their worship is to be referred to their one maker, whom you may properly call the God of gods, as supreme and best." (Hierocles, On the Pythagorean Verses, page 10.)

lemmas.latin: in quantum unum aliquem Deo maximo subditum colit
lemmas.gloss: inasmuch as he worships some one subject to the greatest God
distinct from their author and parent

choices.english: except those whom God wills to be honored
choices.why: Ille is the supreme God of the preceding clause; naming him avoids an ambiguous 'he'.
rejected: unless he wants to be honored

sections.title: So relative intent does not clear the worship given to angels and saints of latria
sections.pass_a: Therefore since the said wise men of the Heathen worshipped the Sun, the Moon and the Genii only with some lower worship, not as highest Gods but only as ministers of the highest God, and referred all that worship to the honor of the highest God himself, as is plain from the testimonies adduced; and nevertheless are said by the apostle to have served the creature, to have shown Latria and divine worship to the creature: it is manifest that those are not cleansed from the crime of Latria shown to Angels and to departed Saints who worship them with prayers and hymns, with vows and oaths conceived by their name, with various offerings, sacred buildings, and feast days dedicated to their honor, even if they protest that they show all those things to the Saints and Angels not as to highest gods, but as to Ministers and friends of God, and so to Gods only by participation, and that relatively to the highest God himself, to whose honor at last those things go and are referred.
pass_b: The pagan philosophers just mentioned worshiped the sun, the moon and the genii only with some lower worship, not as supreme gods but only as servants of the supreme God, and they referred all that worship to the honor of the supreme God himself, as the testimonies cited make plain. Yet the Apostle says that they served the creature, that is, that they gave latria and divine worship to the creature.

It is therefore clear that those who give latria to angels and to departed saints are not cleared of the charge. They worship them with prayers and hymns, with vows and with oaths sworn by their names, with various offerings, and with churches and feast days dedicated to their honor. That holds even if they protest that they give all this to the saints and angels not as to supreme gods, but as to God's servants and friends, and so to gods only by participation, and that relative to the supreme God himself, to whose honor all this finally goes and is referred.

lemmas.gloss: to have served (latreuein) the creature
gods only by participation

choices.english: are not cleared of the charge
choices.why: Purgari a crimine is forensic: to be cleared of an accusation.

sections.title: Not sacrifice alone: Scripture condemns even the sacred kiss (Job 31)
sections.pass_a: Nor is there reason why someone should say that the Heathen are accused by the Apostle of Latria shown to creatures because they offered sacrifices to them, which by the confession of all belong to the worship of Latria. For sacred Scripture condemns the Gentiles not only because they sacrificed to creatures, but even on this account, that they worshipped them with a sacred kiss. From which crime the holy man Job protests that he was free: If I saw, he says, the sun when it shone, and the moon walking brightly; and my heart rejoiced, or rather was enticed, in secret, and I kissed my hand with my mouth. Job 31:26.
pass_b: Nor can anyone say that the reason the Apostle accuses the pagans of giving latria to creatures is that they offered them sacrifices, which everyone admits belong to the worship of latria. For Holy Scripture condemns the Gentiles not only for sacrificing to creatures, but even for worshiping them with a sacred kiss.

The holy man Job protests that he was innocent of this crime: "If I looked at the sun when it shone, and at the moon moving in brightness, and my heart rejoiced, or rather was secretly enticed, and I kissed my hand with my mouth" (Job 31:26-27).

lemmas.gloss: with a sacred kiss
or rather was enticed

choices.term: laetatum est, sive potius seductum est
choices.english: rejoiced, or rather was secretly enticed
choices.why: Le Blanc corrects the Vulgate 'laetatum' by the Hebrew sense 'enticed'; the English keeps his correction.

notes: The 1675 print cites Job 31. 26; the words quoted run through 31:27, so the English cites 31:26-27.
Pass B clarified 2026-10-09: the denial governs the causal clause (quoniam obtulerunt eis sacrificia), not the accusation itself; nemotron misread the earlier wording as a polarity flip.

sections.title: If relative latria is lawful, why not relative sacrifice? The Fathers reserved prayer and hymns too
sections.pass_a: Add that, if according to the hypotheses of the Doctors of the Roman School it is lawful to worship creatures even with Latria, provided not absolute but relative, no solid reason can be rendered why it is not lawful to sacrifice to them relatively. And if it is good and pious to vow vows to Angels and Saints reigning with Christ, and to swear by them, inasmuch as God dwells in them through glory, and divine truth shines out in them, and they are certain Gods by participation, why should it be impious and forbidden, on that title and respect, to offer sacrifices to the same. Nor did the ancient doctors of the Church reserve sacrifices alone to that divine worship which it is unlawful to give to creatures, but, as we saw above, prayers also and hymns, which they want said to the one God, Lord of all things.
pass_b: Besides, if on the premises of the teachers of the Roman school it is lawful to worship creatures even with latria, provided it is relative and not absolute, no solid reason can be given why it should not be lawful to sacrifice to them relatively as well.

If it is good and pious to make vows to the angels and saints who reign with Christ and to swear by them, because God dwells in them by glory, divine truth shines out in them, and they are in a sense gods by participation, why should it be impious and forbidden to offer them sacrifices on that same ground and in that same respect?

Nor did the ancient teachers of the Church reserve only sacrifices for the divine worship that may not be given to creatures. As we saw above, they reserved prayers and hymns as well, which they hold are to be addressed to God alone, the Lord of all.

lemmas.latin: quatenus illis Deus per gloriam inhabitat
lemmas.gloss: inasmuch as God dwells in them by glory
on that ground and in that respect

choices.english: in a sense gods by participation
choices.why: Quidam softens 'gods'; Le Blanc reports the Roman claim, he does not grant it.

sections.title: Colossians 2:18: Paul forbids the threskeia of angels, and so the cult of saints a fortiori
sections.pass_a: But sacred Scripture not only says in general that one God is to be worshipped and that Latria is not to be shown to creatures, but also in particular forbids that we offer any threskeia, that is, any religious worship, to Angels. But if it is not lawful to worship Angels religiously, much less will it be lawful to apply that worship toward departed Saints; since Angels surpass men in excellence of nature, nor are they inferior to the Saints in grace and glory. But the Apostle Paul expressly condemns the threskeia, or religious worship, of Angels. Let no one, he says, seduce you, willing in humility and religion (threskeia) of Angels, walking in the things he has not seen, or setting foot in the things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh. Where the Apostle simply forbids threskeia, that is the religious worship of Angels. But it cannot with any reason be denied that they threskeuein, that is, religiously worship Angels, who build sacred buildings in honor of Angels, dedicate feast days to them, solemnly invoke them in religious places, and seek their patronage and protection with prayers, and as if before them present and looking on bend the knee and fall forward to the ground. And so such men, according to Paul's mind, either have been seduced by those, or are rashly puffed up by the sense of their flesh.
pass_b: Holy Scripture does not only say in general that one God is to be worshiped and that latria is not to be given to creatures. It also forbids in particular that we give any threskeia, that is, any religious worship, to angels. And if it is not lawful to worship angels religiously, much less will it be lawful to give that worship to departed saints, since angels surpass human beings in the excellence of their nature and are not inferior to the saints in grace and glory.

The Apostle Paul expressly condemns the threskeia, or religious worship, of angels: "Let no one lead you astray who delights in humility and the worship of angels, walking in things he has not seen, that is, intruding into things he has not seen, puffed up without reason by the mind of his flesh" (Colossians 2:18). Here the Apostle forbids, without qualification, the threskeia, the religious worship, of angels.

It cannot reasonably be denied that people practice this threskeia, that is, worship angels religiously, when they build churches in honor of angels, dedicate feast days to them, invoke them solemnly in holy places, seek their patronage and protection with prayers, and bend the knee and fall to the ground as if the angels were present and watching. So, on Paul's view, such people have either been led astray by those seducers or are rashly puffed up by the mind of their flesh.

lemmas.gloss: any threskeia (religious worship)
as if before them present and looking on

choices.why: Le Blanc's argument turns on Paul's Greek word, so the English keeps it transliterated and glossed as he does.

notes: Le Blanc quotes Colossians 2:18 without a reference; the English supplies it.

sections.title: Had any angel-cult been lawful, Paul would have distinguished it from the abuse
sections.pass_a: But if any worship of this kind had, in the Apostle's judgment, been owed to Angels, if he had thought it lawful to consecrate feasts and Oratories to Angels, and in the public assemblies of the faithful to sing hymns to them, and to invoke them, and to fall forward before them, he would not simply have condemned the worship of Angels; but if anything immoderate in the religious worship of Angels had been introduced among the Colossians by Impostors, he would have noted that distinctly, and would in some manner have separated the legitimate worship of Angels from the illegitimate: as the Doctors of the Roman School would without doubt do, if any sect should now arise which, in their judgment, attributed something too much to Angels in this kind.
pass_b: If, in the Apostle's judgment, worship of this kind had been owed to angels, and if he had thought it lawful to consecrate feasts and chapels to angels, to sing hymns to them in the public assemblies of the faithful, to invoke them, and to fall down before them, he would not have condemned the worship of angels without qualification.

Had impostors brought some excess into the religious worship of angels among the Colossians, he would have marked it out plainly and would somehow have separated lawful worship of angels from unlawful. That is certainly what the teachers of the Roman school would do if some sect arose now that, in their judgment, gave the angels too much in this respect.

lemmas.gloss: the worship (cultivation) of angels

lemmas.latin: nimium quid Angelis in hoc genere tribueret
lemmas.gloss: attributed something too much to angels in this kind

choices.why: Oratories are small places of prayer; 'chapels' is the plain English.
